messages.content:
Below are all the subtitle lines of a film or TV episode, in order. They will be translated into Spanish in small chunks, by someone who sees only these notes and the chunk.
Write the notes, in English, plain text, at most 300 words:
PEOPLE: each named character: gender, rough age, role, relationship to the others.
ADDRESS: for each pair who talk to each other, the exact Spanish words: what A calls B, and what A calls themself when talking to B, then the same for B. The lines are in another language and won't show these words: choose them yourself from the two people's ages and relationship, as Spanish speakers normally would. Not just "formal" or "informal". Add what changes if their relationship changes during the story. Skip this only if Spanish has no such distinctions.
NAMES: names of people, places and things that must stay spelled the same.
Under PEOPLE, write only what the lines support, and "unknown" where they don't say. Start directly with PEOPLE, no introduction.

You're a jerk, Thom.
Look Celia, we have to follow our passions;
you have your robotics, and I just want to be awesome in space.
Why don't you just admit that you're freaked out by my robot hand?
I'm not freaked out by- it's... alright! Fine!
I'm freaked out! I have nightmares that I'm being chased...
...by these giant robotic claws of death...
Whatever, Thom. We're done.

You translate film and TV subtitles into Spanish. Notes on who is who, made earlier from the whole subtitle file (they can be incomplete, and the lines themselves win if they disagree): """ PEOPLE: Thom: Male, early 20s, aspiring astronaut, Celia’s romantic partner. Seems impulsive and perhaps a little insensitive. Celia: Female, early 20s, robotics engineer, Thom’s romantic partner. Appears grounded and practical. ADDRESS: Thom addresses Celia as "Celia" throughout. When speaking to her, Thom refers to himself as "yo" (I). Celia addresses Thom as "Thom" throughout. When speaking to him, Celia refers to herself as "tú" (you). *Relationship Change Note:* The relationship deteriorates significantly. Initially, the address remains consistent. However, towards the end, the tone shifts, and while the names remain the same, the underlying respect implied by the address diminishes. A translator should convey this through intonation and phrasing, even if the literal "tú" and "Celia" are maintained. A more abrupt shift to a more formal address ("usted") is unlikely given the context, but a noticeable coolness in delivery is appropriate. NAMES: Thom Celia robot """ Use the notes to work out who is probably speaking to whom, then pick gender, forms of address and name spellings that fit, the same way throughout. You get JSON: "lines", numbered subtitle lines to translate, and sometimes "before", the lines just before them, for context only. Answer with JSON only: the same numbers, each with "src", that line copied exactly, and "tr", the translation of that one line. A line is often only part of a sentence that goes on in the next line: translate it as that part, so the lines read naturally one after another, and never move words to another number. Keep , , tags and
line breaks where they belong. Give exactly one translation for each line: never a second version, no "(or: ...)", no notes or explanations. Write natural, spoken Spanish that fits a subtitle: keep names, keep the tone (slang, swearing, formal or informal address) consistent with the context.
